Thermal Inequity in Greater Sydney

Mapping Urban Tree Canopy, Microclimates, and Heat Vulnerability

▷ The East–West Thermal Divide

1. A Tale of Two Sydneys (Surface Temperature)Greater Sydney, summer land surface temperatures reveal a stark geographic divide. While coastal suburbs enjoy cooling sea breezes, inland Western Sydney experiences severe Urban Heat Island (UHI) effects—often reaching 40°C–44°C, well above the metropolitan median of 35.7°C.

2. The Green Canopy Deficittree canopy acts as a vital natural cooling shield. Yet rapid suburban expansion and extensive impervious surfaces across Western and South-Western Sydney have left many neighbourhoods with less than 15% tree cover, compared to the Greater Sydney median of 17.7%.

3. Compounding Socioeconomic Vulnerabilityheat is an environmental justice issue. Overlaying the NSW Heat Vulnerability Index (HVI) with ABS SEIFA disadvantage scores demonstrates that lower-income communities and suburbs with higher shares of elderly residents (aged 65+) disproportionately endure extreme heat with the least green cover.

Data Sources & Methodology Notes

  • Heat Vulnerability Index (2022): Sourced from the NSW SEED Portal (NSW Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure), aggregated from SA1 to SA2 boundaries.
  • Urban Tree Canopy (2024/25): Sourced from the NSW Planning Portal (Greater Sydney Region Tree Canopy 2024/25), representing vegetation cover >3m in height.
  • Socioeconomic & Demographic Indicators (2021): Sourced from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) 2021 Census General Community Profiles (G02) and Socio-Economic Indexes for Areas (SEIFA 2021 IRSD). All datasets share the consistent ASGS Edition 3 (2021) spatial framework.
